display_name: Shafer Vineyards One Point Five, Napa Valley
raw_content:
{
  "hook": "A Napa Valley Cabernet that reads as unapologetically ripe and concentrated — the 2021 and 2022 editions both register 15.3% ABV — One Point Five delivers Napa fruit power without the trophy-bottle price. It trades hillside austerity for broad, immediate dark-fruit presence sourced from across the valley.",
  "wine_summary": "This bottling matters because it packages Napa Valley Cabernet Sauvignon intensity into a single-varietal table wine from a well-known Napa producer. The wine is 100% Cabernet Sauvignon and the recent vintages' high alcohol points to warm-site ripeness that drives the wine's blackberry, black-plum and chocolate notes. Precise vineyard sources and oak regimen for One Point Five are not published, so assessments rely on the wine's sensory profile and Napa Valley context. Napa Valley's mix of valley-floor alluvial soils and volcanic hillside parcels explains why this wine leans toward dense fruit and firm structure rather than lean, mineral restraint.",
  "terroir_expression": "The Napa corridor runs from cool, maritime-influenced northern reaches down to warmer central flats; soils range from deep alluvial Bale loam and Yolo silt loam on the valley floor to volcanic Hambright-series soils in the western Mayacamas and sedimentary Franciscan on the eastern hills. When Napa fruit comes from warmer valley sites and well-drained alluvial benches it produces riper blackcurrant and plum, while any contribution from volcanic hills brings iron and graphite note and firmer tannins — One Point Five tastes like a blend weighted toward the riper valley-fruit end of that spectrum, with underlying structural tannin consistent with some hillside fruit or concentrated extraction.",
  "vinification_summary": "Shafer does not publish detailed winemaking specifics for One Point Five; however, the wine's profile—deep color, ripe tannin and oak spice—aligns with classic Napa Cabernet handling: fermentations that extract phenolics, followed by malolactic fermentation to soften acidity, and time in oak to add vanilla, toast and cedar. Malolactic fermentation (the bacterial conversion of sharper malic acid to softer lactic acid) is important here because it rounds mouthfeel and lets the wine show broader fruit rather than green acidity.",
  "food_pairing": "1) Grilled New York strip with charred bone-marrow butter — the wine's firm tannins cut through the fat while the ripe dark-fruit echoes the beef's caramelized crust.\n2) Braised short ribs in a red-wine reduction (slow-cooked) — the concentrated sauce mirrors the wine's density and the collagen-rich meat softens tannin perception.\n3) Aged English cheddar and toasted sourdough — salt and fat temper tannins and emphasize cassis and dark-chocolate notes for a casual pairing.\n4) Herb-crusted rack of lamb with a black olive tapenade — lamb's gaminess and the tapenade's umami match the wine's black-fruit intensity and graphite-tinged tannic spine.\n5) Grilled portobello mushroom sliders with roasted garlic aioli (casual vegetarian) — the umami and char stand up to the wine's body while the aioli's fat smooths tannin.",
  "comparable_wines": "Silver Oak Napa Valley Cabernet — comparable for oak-forward, plush Napa fruit and a similar retail price band.\nCaymus Napa Valley Cabernet — why it's comparable: lush, high-alcohol Napa fruit profile aimed at early approachability.\nStag's Leap 'Artemis' — comparable for a polished Napa Cabernet profile that balances ripeness and structure.",
  "style_profile": "Cabernet Sauvignon, full-bodied, firm tannins, ripe dark-fruit intensity",
  "cellar_recommendation": "Drink in the near term or cellar for medium-term aging; plan to open between 3 and 12 years from vintage and store at 55°F with steady humidity and minimal light.",
  "value_assessment": "Price: $127–$140 retail. At that price you are paying for Napa Valley Cabernet concentration that sits below the top-tier cult bottles but above entry-level supermarket Cabernets. Comparable buys at similar prices include Silver Oak Napa and certain Caymus bottlings; One Point Five is worth the price if you want a powerful, ready-to-drink Napa Cabernet with strong fruit presence rather than a restrained, cellar-first Bordeaux style.",
  "market_position": "Restaurants and retailers that list reliable Napa Cabernets—steakhouses, hotel wine lists and boutique wine shops—will stock this for guests seeking Napa intensity without chasing three-figure cult scarcity. The audience is drinkers who prioritize bold, fruit-driven Cabernet for immediate enjoyment rather than collectors seeking rarity-driven appreciation.",
  "insider_take": "Treat One Point Five as a high-octane Napa Cabernet built for immediacy: it’s for people who want ripe blackberry, weight and oak spice on release. If you prefer leaner, more mineral-driven Cabernet or long, slow development in the bottle, skip this and instead look to cooler-climate Cabernets from Bordeaux or Coonawarra.",

parsed.food_pairing:
1) Grilled New York strip with charred bone-marrow butter — the wine's firm tannins cut through the fat while the ripe dark-fruit echoes the beef's caramelized crust.
2) Braised short ribs in a red-wine reduction (slow-cooked) — the concentrated sauce mirrors the wine's density and the collagen-rich meat softens tannin perception.
3) Aged English cheddar and toasted sourdough — salt and fat temper tannins and emphasize cassis and dark-chocolate notes for a casual pairing.
4) Herb-crusted rack of lamb with a black olive tapenade — lamb's gaminess and the tapenade's umami match the wine's black-fruit intensity and graphite-tinged tannic spine.
5) Grilled portobello mushroom sliders with roasted garlic aioli (casual vegetarian) — the umami and char stand up to the wine's body while the aioli's fat smooths tannin.
